cim: Colorado Finalizes Automated Decision-Making Technology Rules: Servicing and Collections Are In, and Human Review Gets a Commercial Reasonableness Roadmap
kihagyva: P3: 48 pont, tendencia 20%, jóváhagyás után fordul
cim_eredeti: Colorado Finalizes Automated Decision-Making Technology Rules: Servicing and Collections Are In, and Human Review Gets a Commercial Reasonableness Roadmap
szoveg_eredeti:
The Colorado Attorney General’s office has released the final version of its rules implementing the Automated Decision-Making Technology in Consequential Decisions Act (ADMT Act) and the Conversational Artificial Intelligence Services Act (Chatbot Safety Act). As we reported on October 15 (here), the Colorado Department of Law (DOL) released an interim draft on October 6 after its August 11 initial draft drew more than sixty comments. The final rules keep much of the interim framework, but two changes stand out for financial services institutions: the rules now expressly cover loan servicing and debt collection, and they add detailed language that gives deployers more room to argue that meaningful human review is not commercially reasonable.

Senate Bill 26-189, signed in May 2026, repeals and reenacts the 2024 Colorado artificial intelligence law (Senate Bill 24-205) with new requirements for developers and deployers of automated decision-making technology used in consequential decisions. It takes effect January 1, 2027, and the Attorney General must adopt implementing rules before that date.

The DOL adopted the final rules on November 19, after an October 26 public hearing, but the process is not complete. As the last step, the DOL has requested a formal opinion on the adopted rules from the Attorney General. Once it receives that opinion, the DOL will file the rules and the opinion with the Secretary of State, and the rules will become final 20 days after publication. Because the Attorney General opinion has not yet been issued, the exact date the rules take effect is not yet known.

The final rules revise the definition of “Financial or Lending Service,” as used in § 6-1-1701(6)(d), C.R.S. The definition now lists the following products and services when offered to a consumer: the extension or servicing of credit or a loan, including a consumer credit transaction; transmitting or exchanging funds, including digital assets or through digital wallets; deposit accounts, checking accounts, prepaid cards and debit cards; check cashing; installment payment plans; and debt collection activities.

The DOL added a limiting sentence: nothing in the definition “modifies or expands the scope of covered decisions beyond Consequential Decisions as defined in § 6-1-1701(3), C.R.S.” In our view, that sentence does not solve the problem. Our reading is that the statute’s definition of a Consequential Decision reaches decisions about the provision or denial of financial or lending services, not the back-end servicing and collection of an existing account. The Interim Draft’s example of a bank sending a delinquent credit card account to collections based on a Covered ADMT remains in Rule 7.5, so the DOL appears to treat that scenario as covered. We think that position is not consistent with the statute. Institutions that use models to prioritize accounts for collection, set contact strategies, or offer payment arrangements should evaluate those uses now and should consider whether to raise the issue with the DOL or through other channels.

The statute gives consumers a right to meaningful human review and reconsideration only “to the extent commercially reasonable.” The final rules add substantial detail about how a deployer can make that determination, and much of it is helpful:

There are limits. The rules still treat harm to a basic human need as a heightened consideration, retain a presumption that reconsideration using corrected data is commercially reasonable when it only requires re-running the same ADMT process, and require documentation of reviewer identity, authority, training, evidence and justification. Even so, we expect the financial services industry to invoke the commercial reasonableness exception more regularly, and the DOL’s revised credit card example, in which the store determines that review is commercially reasonable and the reviewer examines the primary evidence, shows what the DOL expects when a deployer does review.

House Bill 26-1263, the Chatbot Safety Act, adds protections for users of conversational AI services and takes effect January 1, 2027. It requires chatbot operators to estimate user age; disclose that users are interacting with AI rather than a human; safeguard teen users against sexually explicit content and simulated emotional dependence; offer privacy and account-management tools for minor users; and maintain suicide and self-harm response protocols. It also bars chatbot outputs from being represented as equivalent to licensed professional services.

Operators must also submit an annual report to the Attorney General that includes “any additional metrics necessary to determine the efficacy and reliability of implemented safeguards or detection, removal, and response protocols, as determined by the attorney general.” The statute does not say more about the report’s content. Although the Chatbot Safety Act does not require rulemaking, the Attorney General has said rules would help make compliance obligations, including the annual report, clear. Financial institutions that deploy customer-facing chatbots should review these requirements alongside the ADMT rules.

With the Attorney General opinion and publication still pending, institutions have a short window to prepare before the law takes effect on January 1, 2027. We recommend that institutions assess their servicing and collections models now and decide whether to press the argument that the DOL’s coverage exceeds the statute, while preparing to comply in the meantime. They should also document commercial reasonableness assessments and any sampling methodology before consumers begin requesting review, since the deployer bears the burden of proof. Institutions with customer-facing chatbots should begin reviewing the Chatbot Safety Act requirements as well. We will continue to monitor the Attorney General opinion and the publication date.
